text: Every dictionary entry carries a Type attribute, and it's the single most consequential choice you make when you add a field. Type decides what the underlying database column actually stores, how the form renders that field to a user, and what further configuration even becomes available to you afterward — a choice list, for instance, only makes sense once Type is set to Choice.

A handful of everyday types cover most of what you'll ever touch. String is plain text, single-line by default, though you can switch it to multi-line and it renders as a text area instead. Integer stores whole numbers — counts, durations in minutes, nothing with a decimal. Boolean, internally called true underscore false, renders as a simple checkbox with exactly two states. Date and Time stores a real timestamp and displays it converted into each viewer's own personal time zone, the same per-user preference from the navigation lab back in Lesson 9. And Choice points at a predefined list of valid values rather than free text — the entire subject of the next lesson.

A Reference field works differently: it doesn't store a value directly at all. It stores the sys_id of a record living on another table, exactly like a foreign key in a relational database. Incident's caller_id field is a Reference into sys_user — the dictionary entry's Reference attribute names sys_user as the target, which is what lets the field render as a searchable lookup instead of a plain text box. Glide List is the closely related multi-value cousin, storing a comma-separated set of sys_ids instead of just one, used for fields like a Watch list where more than one person needs to be linked.

Journal is a type you won't find in a typical database tutorial, and it's distinctly ServiceNow. A Journal field is append-only — every entry a user adds is preserved as its own timestamped, attributed record, instead of overwriting whatever was there before, the way an ordinary String field would. Incident's Additional comments and Work notes fields are both Journal fields, and that's exactly why the Activity formatter shows a running, timestamped history of every comment ever added, by whom, rather than just the single latest one.

A couple more worth knowing: Currency stores an amount together with its currency code, so a value always displays correctly no matter which currency the viewer expects. And Document ID paired with Table Name solves the polymorphic reference problem — a field that needs to point at a record living on any of several different tables, something one ordinary, fixed-target Reference field simply can't express on its own. Next up: how Choice lists are actually built and configured.
